clinicalPearls: An autosomal recessive disorder of L-serine biosynthesis caused by deficiency of phosphoglycerate dehydrogenase
The classic infantile form presents with congenital microcephaly, intractable seizures and severe psychomotor retardation
Milder juvenile forms with absence seizures and developmental delay are recognised
The most severe end of the spectrum overlaps with Neu-Laxova syndrome
Cerebrospinal fluid and, to a lesser extent, plasma show low serine (and often low glycine)
It is one of the treatable inborn errors — oral serine (with glycine) supplementation can improve seizures and, if started early, outcomes
Serine is essential for neuronal membrane, neurotransmitter and one-carbon metabolism, explaining the neurological phenotype
reference.pathophysiology: Phosphoglycerate dehydrogenase catalyses the first committed step of de novo L-serine synthesis from a glycolytic intermediate. Deficiency limits endogenous serine production, which is critical in the brain because serine crosses the blood-brain barrier poorly and neural tissue depends heavily on local synthesis. Serine is a precursor for glycine, phospholipids, nucleotides and D-serine (an NMDA-receptor co-agonist), so its deficiency impairs myelination, neuronal proliferation and neurotransmission, producing microcephaly, seizures and developmental impairment. Providing exogenous serine bypasses the enzymatic block.
additionalDifferentials: Other serine biosynthesis defects (phosphoserine aminotransferase or phosphatase deficiency)
Congenital microcephaly of other genetic cause
Neu-Laxova syndrome (severe end of the spectrum)
additionalInvestigations: Plasma and cerebrospinal fluid amino acids showing low serine
Brain MRI (may show hypomyelination and cortical atrophy)
Assessment of the other serine-pathway enzymes if PHGDH is normal
redFlags: Congenital microcephaly with intractable neonatal seizures
Feeding difficulties and failure to thrive
Severe presentation overlapping with Neu-Laxova syndrome
reference.prognosis: Untreated classic disease carries a poor neurological prognosis; early serine (and glycine) supplementation can markedly reduce seizures and, when started antenatally or in early infancy, may substantially improve outcome.
pitfalls: Measuring only plasma amino acids, as cerebrospinal fluid serine is more sensitive
Overlooking a treatable cause of a neonatal epileptic encephalopathy
Delaying a trial of serine supplementation while awaiting genetics
Confusing it with non-treatable causes of congenital microcephaly
references: Textbook of Inborn Metabolic Diseases (standard reference)
management: Provide lifelong oral L-serine supplementation, usually with added glycine, to bypass the enzymatic block and replenish central serine
Start supplementation as early as possible, including antenatally in affected pregnancies, to maximise neurological outcome
Control seizures with appropriate anticonvulsant therapy alongside serine replacement
Support development with physiotherapy, occupational therapy and speech and language input
Monitor cerebrospinal fluid and plasma serine and glycine and titrate supplementation against clinical and biochemical response
Offer genetic counselling with PHGDH cascade testing of the family and prenatal diagnosis for future pregnancies
Coordinate care through metabolic medicine and paediatric neurology
